editorial.headline: Compound Fertiliser Production With a Bali Scope Test
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers macro-nutrient fertiliser manufacturing that is nationally foreign-open, while Bali depends on the exact OSS risk scope declared.
editorial.body:
This KBLI activity is for producers making fertiliser built around primary macro nutrients, especially products that contain at least two of those nutrients. The record describes two manufacturing routes. One is chemical reaction, with examples such as monoammonium phosphate, potassium ammonium chloride, potassium metaphosphate, and ammonium potassium phosphate. The other is physical blending, where fertilisers are mixed without changing the original chemical nature or fertiliser properties. The scope also reaches secondary macro-nutrient fertilisers containing calcium, magnesium, and sulphur, including examples such as kieserite and magnesium oxide.

In practical terms, this is not a trading label or a broad agriculture catch-all. It is a manufacturing classification for businesses whose activity is the making of compound or secondary macro-nutrient fertiliser products. The scale field is unusually broad: the record opens it to Mikro, Kecil, Menengah, and Besar operators. That means the activity can be registered across the full enterprise-size spectrum shown in the record, from micro through large-scale businesses, provided the declared activity remains inside the manufacturing scope described above.

The national investment picture is clear. The PMA status is marked TERBUKA, and the foreign-ownership ceiling is 100%, with the source listed as Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. Nationally, then, this is a foreign-open activity at the full ceiling stated in the record. There is no lower percentage to infer, no special capital number to add, and no hidden licence condition supplied here. The honest reading is simply that the national field allows foreign ownership up to 100% for this activity.

Bali is more careful. The record does not mark the code as fully blocked; l4_bali_blocked is false. But the Bali status is Blocked (scope-dependent), and the stated reason is specific: “OSS risk at scale Besar is low on SOME scope(s) but higher on other(s): registrable as PMA in Bali only by declaring the higher-risk scope (e.g. PPMSE for platform-trade codes) — verify live OSS per exact activity.” The moratorium rule also matters because the record says Bali province blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk KBLI for PMA, island-wide and permanently. So the editorial conclusion is narrow but important: this activity is nationally open to PMA, yet in Bali the registration outcome depends on the exact declared OSS activity and risk scope. A founder should not treat the national 100% ceiling as automatic Bali registrability; the live OSS declaration must carry the higher-risk scope needed for Bali, if the exact activity supports it.
